influences/holy-wells-sacred-places/name: Holy wells, springs and sacred places
influences/holy-wells-sacred-places/sour: Veneration of springs, wells, trees, stones and hilltops with votive offerings
influences/holy-wells-sacred-places/chri: Holy wells dedicated to saints, patterns and pilgrimages, healing springs and well-dressing
influences/holy-wells-sacred-places/evid: Pre-Christian water cults are archaeologically certain (Bath, Coventina’s Well) and church councils repeatedly condemned worship at springs and trees, so some continuity is likely. But most individual holy wells are first documented in the medieval or modern period, and historians such as James Rattue and Ronald Hutton warn that a pagan origin for any particular well is usually assumed rather than proven.
influences/holy-wells-sacred-places/popu: Every holy well is an ancient pagan sacred spring that the church simply renamed after a saint.
influences/holy-wells-sacred-places/what: Sacred springs were common in the Roman and Celtic world: thousands of coins were found in Coventina’s Well at Carrawburgh on Hadrian’s Wall, and the hot spring at Bath was the shrine of Sulis Minerva. Early medieval councils and preachers — the Second Council of Arles (c. 452), Caesarius of Arles, Martin of Braga (c. 572), the Council of Tours (567) and later English laws of Edgar and Cnut — condemned people who lit candles or made vows at springs, trees and stones, which shows that such practices continued. At the same time Gregory the Great urged missionaries to Christianise rather than destroy holy places. Yet the documentary record for most wells starts in the twelfth century or later, and many were dedicated to saints with no pre-Christian connection, or became holy because of a later miracle or a nearby church. Victorian folklorists tended to read every survival as pagan; modern scholars find a mixture of genuine continuity, Christian invention and modern revival.
influences/holy-wells-sacred-places/summ: Christianity inherited a landscape full of sacred springs and places. Church leaders both condemned worship at them and baptised them as saints’ wells, but the pagan origin of individual wells is usually hard to prove.
influences/holy-wells-sacred-places/stor:
The pre-Christian peoples of the Mediterranean and of Celtic and Germanic Europe treated springs, rivers, groves and stones as places of divine presence. Roman Britain provides some of the clearest evidence: the hot spring at Bath (Aquae Sulis) was the sanctuary of Sulis Minerva, where worshippers threw curse tablets into the water, and Coventina’s Well at Carrawburgh on Hadrian’s Wall yielded thousands of coins, altars and other offerings. Similar votive deposits are known from Gaul and Germany.

Church councils in the West spent centuries trying to stop these practices. The Second Council of Arles (c. 452, canon 23) condemned those who ‘light torches or venerate trees, springs or stones’; Caesarius of Arles (died 542) preached repeatedly against vows at trees and springs; Martin of Braga’s On the Correction of Peasants (c. 572) listed lighting candles at stones, trees and springs among the devil’s works. In England the laws of King Edgar and of Cnut (1020s) still prohibited ‘well-worship’.

Alongside condemnation ran adaptation. Gregory the Great’s letter to Mellitus (601, Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.30) advised that temples be purified and reused, and that the people be allowed their feasts in honour of the saints. In Ireland, Scotland, Wales and Cornwall hundreds of wells bear saints’ names; legends tell of springs bursting forth where a saint prayed or where a martyr’s head fell. St Winefride’s Well at Holywell in North Wales, whose Life was written by Robert of Shrewsbury about 1138, has been a pilgrimage site ever since and was one of the few shrines to survive the English Reformation in continuous use.

The question is how much of this is continuity. In Ireland, Máire MacNeill’s The Festival of Lughnasa (1962) made a strong case that late-summer assemblies at hilltops and wells — including the Reek Sunday pilgrimage on Croagh Patrick — preserve a pre-Christian harvest festival. But James Rattue’s survey of English holy wells and Ronald Hutton’s work on British paganism show that most wells are first recorded long after conversion, that dedications were often medieval or even post-Reformation, and that customs such as Derbyshire well-dressing or the rag-hung ‘clootie wells’ of Scotland are attested only from the early modern period.

Protestant reformers treated wells as superstition: Henry VIII’s injunctions of 1538 attacked pilgrimages to wells and images, and Scottish Kirk sessions disciplined people for visiting wells in the seventeenth century. Catholic Ireland, Brittany and Galicia kept the ‘patterns’ (patron-saint days) at wells, and new healing springs such as Lourdes (1858) show that the Christian sense of holy water in a place did not depend on pagan precedent. Today holy wells attract both Christian pilgrims and modern pagans, who sometimes claim them as survivals of the old religion.

Reformers suppressed well pilgrimages; Catholic regions kept patterns, and folk customs revived in the modern period.

influences/all-saints-samhain/name: All Saints, All Souls, Halloween and Samhain
influences/all-saints-samhain/sourceCult: The Gaelic Samhain (1 November), a seasonal assembly and feast marking the start of winter
influences/all-saints-samhain/christianF: All Saints (1 November), All Souls (2 November) and the popular customs of All Hallows' Eve
influences/all-saints-samhain/evidenceNo: The Christian feast of all martyrs and saints grew from Eastern and Roman commemorations with no Celtic link. Examples are Chrysostom's sermon for the Sunday after Pentecost, the Pantheon's dedication on 13 May 609, and Gregory III's oratory to all saints. The move to 1 November is first clearly attested in eighth-century Rome and Anglo-Saxon/Frankish circles. Irish martyrologies, by contrast, kept all saints on 20 April. A Samhain influence on the date is possible but unproven. Some later Halloween folk customs in Ireland and Scotland may preserve Samhain associations. Others are early-modern or American.
influences/all-saints-samhain/popularCla: Halloween is the ancient Celtic festival of the dead, Samhain, and the church moved All Saints to 1 November to Christianise it.
influences/all-saints-samhain/whatHistor: Ronald Hutton and Nicholas Rogers stress how thin the evidence for pre-Christian Samhain is. It appears in medieval Irish literature as a 1 November assembly with feasting and supernatural incidents, but nothing shows that it was a festival of the dead or a 'Celtic New Year'. Those ideas were largely shaped by John Rhŷs and James Frazer around 1890. All Saints on 1 November is first clearly attested in Rome under Gregory III (731–41) and in the circle of Alcuin and Arno of Salzburg (c.800). Gregory IV and Louis the Pious extended it across the Frankish empire in 835. Because the early Irish church kept the feast in April, the Samhain-substitution theory is doubtful, though not impossible. All Souls on 2 November was introduced by Odilo of Cluny c.998 and is a monastic development. Halloween customs such as souling, guising, turnip lanterns and later trick-or-treating developed in Christian and early-modern Britain and Ireland and in twentieth-century North America.
influences/all-saints-samhain/summary: All Saints and All Souls are Christian commemorations of the dead whose November dates were fixed in the eighth to tenth centuries. Whether the choice of 1 November had anything to do with the Gaelic Samhain is debated, and the notion of Halloween as an ancient Celtic 'festival of the dead' is largely a modern construction.
influences/all-saints-samhain/story:
Commemorating all martyrs together was an Eastern custom before it was a Western one. Syriac sources and Ephrem's circle knew a feast of all martyrs in the Easter season. John Chrysostom preached on 'all the martyrs of the whole world' on the Sunday after Pentecost, still the Orthodox Sunday of All Saints. In Rome, Pope Boniface IV received the Pantheon from the emperor Phocas and on 13 May 609 or 610 dedicated it to St Mary and all martyrs (Santa Maria ad Martyres). It is one of the clearest cases of a temple becoming a church.

The 1 November date appears in the eighth century. The Liber Pontificalis records that Gregory III (731–41) built an oratory in St Peter's for the relics 'of all the saints'. Its anniversary may have been 1 November. Around 800 Alcuin wrote of a 1 November feast of all saints kept in Frankish and English circles. In 835 Gregory IV persuaded Louis the Pious to proclaim it throughout the Frankish realm. Meanwhile the Irish Félire Óengusso (c.800) commemorated all the saints of Europe on 20 April. That is one reason Hutton suggests the November date may have come from Germanic Europe rather than Ireland.

All Souls was a monastic innovation. Abbot Odilo of Cluny (c.998) ordered his houses to pray for all the faithful departed on 2 November, the day after All Saints. Rome adopted the observance by the thirteenth century. With the growth of purgatory doctrine, All Hallows' Eve, All Saints and All Souls (Hallowtide) became a season of bell-ringing, candles and prayers for the dead. Later the poor went 'souling' for soul-cakes in return for prayers.

The Reformation broke much of this up. Protestant reformers abolished prayers for the dead and All Souls, though Anglicans and Lutherans kept All Saints. In Protestant England some customs were transferred to Guy Fawkes Night (5 November). In Ireland and Highland Scotland, Samhain/Halloween folklore survived, including divination, guising and turnip lanterns. Antiquarians such as Rhŷs and Frazer then interpreted these customs as pagan relics. Irish and Scottish emigrants took Halloween to North America, where trick-or-treating and pumpkin jack-o'-lanterns became standard in the 1920s–50s.

Today Catholics and Anglicans keep All Saints and All Souls. The Orthodox commemorate the departed on 'soul Saturdays' and All Saints after Pentecost. Lutherans and many Protestants observe Reformation Day on 31 October. Some evangelical and Pentecostal groups reject Halloween as occult or pagan. Modern Pagans revived Samhain as a festival of the dead, partly on the basis of Frazer's theories.
influences/all-saints-samhain/howItHappe: Eastern churches commemorated all martyrs on a single day in the Easter season (Edessa, Antioch, Constantinople).
Boniface IV dedicated the Pantheon to Mary and all martyrs (609/610).
Gregory III's oratory 'of all saints' in St Peter's and Anglo-Frankish usage (c.800) fixed 1 November.
Louis the Pious, at Gregory IV's request, extended the feast through the Frankish empire (835).
Odilo of Cluny added All Souls on 2 November (c.998), and late-medieval and early-modern folk customs grew around All Hallows' Eve.

His policy of adapting pagan sites and festivals (601) is often cited, though without direct evidence, as the model for a Christian Samhain.
influences/all-saints-samhain/critics/0/: Rejected prayers for the dead and purgatory, abolishing All Souls in most Protestant churches. Luther's Ninety-Five Theses were posted on All Hallows' Eve 1517.
